titles.695: Man. Post. Cap. X: GAR — tree gone, but the ban’s punishing force still reaches posterity (cross parallel)
titles.696: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — law’s force is mandate or threat; the mandate neither lasts nor reaches us
titles.697: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — ‘you eat / you die’ both address Adam, not all posterity
titles.698: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — if Adam alone had died that day, the threat was still satisfied
titles.699: Man. Post. Cap. X: PLAC — Christ became a curse (Gal 3:13), not by that ban’s force but by gospel grace
titles.700: Man. Post. Cap. X tip — Christ’s cross-merit comes by free imputation, not by the Deuteronomy hanging-law

latin.695: GAR. Ad argumentationem, lex illa iam ab aliquot annorum millibus non est amplius &c. Resp. Nec Arborem exstare amplius, neque adeo legem illam perdurare, quatenus respiciebat prohibitionem fructus illius vetiti; sed vim tamen legis perseverare, quatenus inobedientiae illi Adami punitionem interminabatur quae non Adamo tantum incubitura, verum etiam in omnes posteros dimanatura esset. Sicut etiam Christus in arbore Crucis direptus est, & ibi maledictionem pertulit, ex vi & praescripto legis illius a Deo constitutae, Maledictus qui pendet in ligno, ut docet Paulus Galat. iii. 13. Sublata est Crux, & lex illa non perdurat; & tamen obedientiae, quam Christus in maledicta illa Cruce praestitit, meritum ad nos imputatione gratuita dimanat, & ad mundi finem dimanaturum est.
latin.696: PLAC. Nec distinctionem illam legis, nec verba quibus concepta est, exagitabo; tantum dicam vim legis vel in mandato, vel in comminatione spectari. Illam nec perseverare, nec ad nos pertinere certum est. Hanc ad nos pertinere nec probat Vir doctus, nec quomodo probari possit intelligo.
latin.697: Nihil enim est in verbis comminationis, ex quo deduci possit, eam ad alios spectare, quam ad quos spectat mandatum seu interdictum. Quo die comederis ex ea, morte morieris. Quis non videt ad eandem personam utrumque illud verbum comederis & morieris spectare, non autem hoc ad omnes homines, illud ad solum Adamum?
latin.698: An est sensus, Quo die tu & omnes posteri tui comederitis ex ea, tu & posteri tui moriemini? Non certe; nemo enim posterorum Adami ex ea comedit. Num igitur est sensus, Quo die tu comederis ex ea, eo die morte morieris tu & omnes posteri tui? Quis non videt verba & omnes posteri tui afficticia esse, nec magis contineri in verbo morieris, quam in verbo comederis? Quod si eo die mortuus fuisset Adam, ut merebatur eius peccatum, morte corporis & aeterna, quam unius fuisset peccatum, tam unius fuisset punitio, & tamen satisfactum fuisset legis comminationi. Exemplum Christi, qui, ut vas noster, loco nostro punitus est, iam aliquoties ostendi nihil iuvare imputationem immediatam primae Adami actualis inobedientiae.
latin.699: Miror autem unde habuerit Vir doctus, Christum in cruce maledictionem pertulisse ex vi & praescripto legis illius a Deo constitutae, Maledictus qui pendet in ligno. Docet quidem Paulus Gal. iii. 13. Christum pro nobis factum esse maledictionem, idque probat quia pependit in ligno, & scriptum est, Maledictus quisquis pendet in ligno. Sed non docet factum fuisse maledictionem ex vi & praescripto illius legis.
latin.700: Nulla enim lex fuit quae iuberet Christum in crucem agi, nec sic nobis imputatio obedientiae a Christo in maledicta illa cruce praestitae est secundum illam legem, aut secundum legem, sed ex mera gratia, secundum promissiones Evangelii.

pass_a.695: Garissoles answers the ‘law is gone’ point: the tree is gone, so the ban no longer lasts as a fruit-prohibition; yet the law’s force still lasts as the threat of punishing Adam’s disobedience—and that punishment was to lie not on Adam only but to flow to all posterity. So too Christ on the cross-tree bore the curse by the force of ‘cursed is he who hangs on a tree’ (Gal 3:13). The cross is gone and that law does not last; yet the merit of the obedience he rendered on that cursed cross flows to us by free imputation to the world’s end.
pass_a.696: Placeus will not quarrel over the distinction’s wording: a law’s force is seen either in the mandate or in the threat. That the mandate neither lasts nor reaches us is certain. That the threat reaches us the learned man neither proves nor shows how it could be proved.
pass_a.697: Nothing in the threat’s words lets it cover others than those the mandate covers. ‘In the day you eat of it, you shall die.’ Who does not see that both ‘you eat’ and ‘you die’ address the same person—not ‘die’ to all men and ‘eat’ to Adam alone?
pass_a.698: Is the sense ‘the day you and all your posterity eat, you and they die’? No—none of Adam’s posterity ate of it. Or ‘the day you eat, you and all your posterity die that day’? Who does not see ‘and all your posterity’ is tacked on, no more in ‘you die’ than in ‘you eat’? If Adam had died that day in body and eternally as his sin deserved, the sin would have been one man’s and the punishment one man’s—and the threat would still have been satisfied. Christ’s example as our surety punished in our place has already been shown to give no help to immediate imputation of Adam’s first actual disobedience.
pass_a.699: Placeus wonders where the learned man got that Christ bore the curse on the cross by the force and prescription of ‘cursed is he who hangs on a tree.’ Paul does teach (Gal 3:13) that Christ was made a curse for us, proving it because he hung on a tree and it is written, cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree. But he does not teach that Christ was made a curse by that law’s force and prescription.
pass_a.700: No statute ordered Christ to the cross. So the obedience he rendered on that cursed tree is not counted to us by that hanging-law, or by law at all, but solely by grace under the Gospel promises.

695: GAR. To the argumentation that that law for some thousands of years now is no more, etc., the reply is: neither does the Tree still stand, nor therefore does that law endure insofar as it regarded the prohibition of that forbidden fruit; yet the force of the law still perseveres insofar as it threatened punishment for that disobedience of Adam which was to lie not on Adam only, but also to flow out upon all posterity.

Just as Christ too was taken on the tree of the Cross, and there bore the curse, by the force and prescription of that law constituted by God, Cursed is he who hangs on a tree, as Paul teaches in Galatians 3:13.

The Cross has been taken away, and that law does not endure; and yet the merit of the obedience which Christ rendered on that cursed Cross flows to us by free imputation, and will flow to the end of the world.
696: PLAC. I will not quarrel over that distinction of the law, nor over the words in which it is framed; I will only say that the force of a law is regarded either in the mandate or in the threat.
That the former neither perseveres nor pertains to us is certain.
That the latter pertains to us the learned man neither proves, nor do I see how it can be proved.
697: For there is nothing in the words of the threat from which it can be deduced that it looks to others than those to whom the mandate or ban looks.
In the day you eat of it, you shall die the death.
Who does not see that both that word you eat and you die look to the same person—not this to all men, and that to Adam alone?
698: Is the sense, In the day you and all your posterity eat of it, you and your posterity shall die? Certainly not; for none of Adam’s posterity ate of it.
Is the sense then, In the day you eat of it, on that day you shall die the death—you and all your posterity?
Who does not see that the words and all your posterity are tacked on, and are no more contained in the word you die than in the word you eat?

But if on that day Adam had died, as his sin deserved, with the death of the body and the eternal death, as the sin would have been of one, so the punishment would have been of one—and yet the threat of the law would have been satisfied.
The example of Christ, who as our surety was punished in our place, I have already several times shown helps nothing the immediate imputation of Adam’s first actual disobedience.
699: But I wonder where the learned man got it that Christ on the cross bore the curse by the force and prescription of that law constituted by God, Cursed is he who hangs on a tree.
Paul does teach in Galatians 3:13 that Christ was made a curse for us, and proves it because he hung on a tree, and it is written, Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.
But he does not teach that he was made a curse by the force and prescription of that law.
700: For there was no law which ordered that Christ be driven to the cross; nor is the imputation to us of the obedience rendered by Christ on that cursed cross according to that law, or according to law, but from mere grace, according to the promises of the Gospel.
